notes.h: What a business model is and the five common ones
notes.b: A business model is an element within the business plan which outlines how a company will operate, create, deliver, and capture value in economic, social, and cultural contexts. In practice, the quickest way to tell models apart is to ask how each one earns its income.
points: Five common models are retail, manufacturing, subscription, franchise and affiliate, and each one earns money in a different way.

Three terms recur: revenue (money coming in from customers), mark-up (the amount added to the purchase cost to set the selling price) and scalability (the ability to grow without a matching rise in costs).
A manufacturer makes goods, a wholesaler buys in bulk and sells on, and a retailer sells to the final consumer, so the three sit at different points in the chain from raw material to customer.
notes.tip: For any model, say how it earns money first, then give a feature tied to cost, control, risk or scalability. In an identify question, name the model and the feature that shows it, such as a recurring fee, a brand licence or a commission.

notes.b: A retail business sells finished goods directly to end consumers, usually buying them in from manufacturers or wholesalers. It is the model most people meet every day in shops and online.
points: It earns income by selling goods above their purchase cost, so profit depends on the mark-up applied and the volume sold.
Key features include a shop or online store, a range of goods chosen for the target market and direct contact with customers.
Advantage: direct feedback from customers, so the retailer can see quickly what sells and what does not.
Advantages: wide reach through a high-street or online presence, and flexibility in choosing what to stock, so the range can change as demand changes.
Disadvantages: the costs of premises and stock are high, and competition is intense because customers can easily switch to another shop.
Another disadvantage: sales fall quickly when consumer spending weakens, while rent and stock costs still have to be paid.

Example: Tesco Ireland, a supermarket chain, sells groceries and other goods bought from manufacturers and wholesalers to consumers, and also offers online grocery shopping with home delivery and Click+Collect.
notes.tip: Retail buys goods in and sells them on; manufacturing makes the goods. If a firm does both, keep its main model clear in your answer.

notes.b: A manufacturing business converts raw materials or components into finished products, which it sells to retailers or other businesses. Unlike a retailer, it makes what it sells.
points: It earns income by selling what it makes at a price that covers production costs and leaves a profit margin.
Key features include factories or plants, machinery, skilled labour and direct control over quality and production processes.
Advantages: control over the product and its quality, because the firm decides how the goods are made.
Advantages: the possibility of lower unit costs at high volume, since fixed costs are spread over more units, and the ability to build a brand.
Disadvantages: heavy investment in equipment and buildings is needed before anything can be sold.
Disadvantages: machinery can become obsolete (out of date), and the firm is exposed to changing raw material prices, which can squeeze its margin.

Example: Kerry Group, headquartered in Tralee, Co. Kerry, makes food ingredients and sells largely to other businesses as a business-to-business taste and nutrition company, supplying food, beverage and pharmaceutical customers.
notes.tip: A manufacturer may also sell directly to consumers, but name the main model: it makes goods. Link manufacturing to high fixed costs and to growth that needs new plant and equipment.

notes.b: A subscription business charges customers a recurring fee for continued access to a product or service, rather than making a one-off sale. The customer keeps paying for as long as they want access.
points: It earns income through regular payments, which make revenue more predictable and easier to forecast than one-off sales.
Key features include an ongoing relationship with customers, access that is renewed monthly or annually and a strong focus on keeping existing customers.
Advantages: predictable income, which helps the business plan and forecast, and data about customer usage that helps it target offers.
Advantage: a lower cost of earning repeat business, because keeping a subscriber is cheaper than winning a new customer each time.
Disadvantages: customers can cancel easily, so the business must keep delivering value or lose them.
Disadvantage: early costs can be high before enough subscribers join to cover them.
Example: Spotify charges a monthly fee for its premium music service, which removes adverts and allows offline listening.
notes.tip: Do not describe a loyalty scheme as a subscription. A subscription is a recurring payment for access, not a reward for buying.

notes.b: In a franchise arrangement, a franchisor licenses its brand, system and know-how to independent franchisees, who run outlets in return for fees. The franchisee runs its own outlet under someone else's brand.
points: The franchisor earns income from fees paid by franchisees, and the franchisee earns its profit from its own outlet after paying those fees.
Key features include a proven business system, a shared brand, training and support from the franchisor and standardised products.
Advantage for the franchisee: an established brand and system lower the risk of starting a business, although the franchisee gives up some freedom.
Advantage for the franchisor: rapid expansion with less capital, since franchisees fund their own outlets.
Disadvantage: the franchisor loses some control over local outlets, because independent owners run them day to day.
Disadvantage: a poorly run outlet can damage the brand for every franchisee, since customers judge the brand as a whole.
Example: Subway operates in Ireland through outlets run by independent owners under a franchise agreement.
notes.tip: Franchise and affiliate are easily confused. A franchisee runs its own outlet under the franchisor's brand and pays fees; an affiliate sells nothing itself and is paid commission for sending customers to another firm.

notes.b: The two parties in a franchise have different roles, obligations and levels of risk, and their fees and royalties reflect this. Keeping each party's income, duties and risk separate is the key to this topic.
points: The franchisor provides the brand, operating system, training and supply arrangements, and it keeps ownership of the brand.
The franchisee provides the premises, most of the capital and local management, and must follow the franchisor's standards.
Fees: an initial fee is paid once to join, and royalties are paid regularly, usually as a share of the outlet's sales.
Control: the franchisor sets rules on products, pricing and appearance, which limits how far the franchisee can make its own decisions.
Risk: the franchisee carries most of the financial risk of the outlet, because it funds the premises and capital, while the franchisor's main risk is damage to its brand reputation.
notes.tip: Do not give only the franchisee's advantages. A full answer gives both sides, the payment structure (initial fee and royalties) and the effect on risk and control. Do not confuse the initial fee (paid once) with royalties (paid regularly).

notes.b: An affiliate business earns commission by promoting another firm's products and sending customers to it, usually through a tracked link. The affiliate does not sell or deliver anything itself.
points: Income is earned as commission on each sale or lead the affiliate generates, so the affiliate is paid only when a result occurs.
Key features include a tracked referral link, which records which customers the affiliate sent, reliance on a website, social media channel or blog, and no need to hold stock.
Advantages: low start-up costs, little or no need for premises or stock, and the ability to work from home.
Disadvantages: income depends on the merchant's programme terms (the rules set by the firm whose products are promoted), which can change.
Disadvantage: commission rates are often modest.
Example: a sample business is a blogger who reviews kitchen appliances and earns commission on sales made through links on the review page.
notes.tip: The signal for an affiliate in a question is commission on referrals through a link. If the business runs its own outlet under another firm's brand, it is a franchise instead.

notes.b: The five models differ on revenue, cost, control, risk and scalability, so a business should choose the model that fits its goals and resources. Comparing under these five headings, and referring to both models under each, gives a clear answer.
points: Revenue: subscription gives predictable recurring income, while retail and manufacturing depend on each individual sale.
Cost: retail and manufacturing carry high fixed costs, whereas an affiliate has very low costs and a franchisor's own costs are modest.
Control: retail and manufacturing give the owner full control over the offer, while franchise and affiliate models depend on others.
Risk: retail and manufacturing carry more financial risk because of stock and capital tied up, while an affiliate risks very little money.
Scalability: franchising and affiliate models can grow quickly with less capital, while manufacturing growth requires new plant and equipment.
notes.tip: In a compare question, do not describe each model in turn. Use headings such as revenue, cost, control, risk and scalability and refer to both models under each one.

notes.b: Each model raises its own ethical and sustainability questions, and technology shapes how each one operates. Applying these to a business in a question shows the effect on customers and reputation.
points: Ethics: franchisors must be honest about costs and support when recruiting franchisees, so people do not invest on false promises.
Ethics: affiliates must disclose that they earn commission, so their recommendations are honest and readers can judge them fairly.
Ethics: subscription businesses should make cancelling easy and billing clear, so customers are not trapped in payments they did not intend.
Sustainability: retailers and manufacturers can reduce waste and packaging, source responsibly and design for repair and recycling.
Sustainability: manufacturers also face raw material and energy impacts, because making goods uses resources.
Digital: retail can sell online as well as in store, and subscriptions are managed through apps and online accounts.
Digital: affiliate marketing depends on tracked online links and data, which show which sales the affiliate generated.
notes.tip: When a question asks you to apply ethics, sustainability or digital tools to a model, state the effect on customers or reputation, such as honest disclosure building trust.

keyTerms.definition: Selling finished goods directly to end consumers through a shop or online store.
Converting raw materials or components into finished products that are sold to retailers or other businesses.
A business model that charges a recurring fee for ongoing access to a product or service.
A licensing arrangement in which a brand owner lets independent operators trade under its name and system in return for fees.
The business that owns a brand and system and licenses them to independent operators.
The independent operator who runs an outlet under a brand owner's name, paying fees and following its standards.
A regular payment, often a share of sales, that an operator makes to a brand owner for continued use of its brand and system.
A business model that earns commission by referring customers to another firm's products through a tracked link.
The payment, usually a percentage of a sale, that an affiliate earns for sending a customer to a merchant.

factCards.definition: Retail, manufacturing, subscription, franchise and affiliate.

factCards.term: Main advantage of the affiliate model
factCards.definition: Low start-up cost, little or no stock and the ability to grow without fixed premises.
High capital investment in plant and equipment, plus exposure to changes in raw material prices.
A proven brand and system lower the risk of failure, but the franchisee gives up freedom over products and prices.
Predictable recurring income that is easier to forecast than income from one-off sales.

questions.prompt: Compare the franchise model with the retail model on revenue, cost, control, risk and scalability, for an owner deciding which model to adopt.
questions.model: Revenue: a retailer earns from each sale, so its profit depends on margins and footfall. A franchisee earns similar sales in its outlet, but the franchisor earns fees that do not depend on the outlet's profit, so the franchisor's revenue is steadier. Cost: a retailer pays for premises, stock and staff from its own capital. A franchisee pays the same operating costs but also pays initial fees and royalties on top. Control: a retailer decides its products, prices and design, while a franchisee must follow the franchisor's system and standards. Risk: a retailer carries the full risk of an unsuccessful shop, whereas a franchisee benefits from a proven system, which lowers the risk of failure though does not remove it. Scalability: a retailer grows mainly by opening more shops funded from its own capital, while a franchisor can expand quickly because franchisees fund new outlets. An owner who wants independence may prefer retail, while one who wants a proven system with less risk may prefer a franchise.

questions.prompt: Explain how a franchisor earns income, and describe two advantages and two disadvantages of the franchise model for the franchisee.
questions.model: A franchisor earns an initial fee from each franchisee when the outlet opens, and ongoing royalties, usually calculated as a share of the outlet's sales. One advantage for the franchisee is access to an established brand and proven system, which lowers the risk of a new business failing. A second advantage is training and support from the franchisor, which helps an inexperienced owner run the outlet. One disadvantage is that the franchisee must pay fees and royalties, which reduce its profit even when the outlet trades well. A second disadvantage is loss of freedom, because the franchisee must follow the franchisor's rules on products, prices and appearance.
